findings.claim: The test suite added alongside this refactor never exercises the "masked_text" kind, plain or Packed, even though CHANGES.md explicitly claims the refactor preserves encoding behavior for every kind that used to be picked up, and should_encode's categorical set is {"text", "masked_text", "choice"} -- one of the three named kinds is untested in both its plain and packed form.
findings.source: test_columnstore.py:17-26 (`_table()` only builds "text"/"number"/"choice" columns plus Packed("text")/Packed("choice") -- no "masked_text" or Packed("masked_text") column exists anywhere in the file) and CHANGES.md:7-10 ("so every column kind that used to be picked up by the alias-list call is still picked up here, and nothing else is. No change in which columns get encoded.")
findings.remedy: Add a `Column("notes", "masked_text", [...])` and a `Column("packed_notes", Packed("masked_text"), [...])` to `_table()` and assert both land in `encode_categoricals`'s result, so the test suite actually backs the parity claim the changelog makes instead of leaving 1 of 3 categorical kinds unverified.

findings.claim: column_subset is defined but has no caller and no test anywhere in the given source -- encode_categoricals now calls should_encode directly, and test_columnstore.py's import list omits column_subset entirely -- yet the module docstring asserts it "remains the general-purpose way to pick columns by kind elsewhere in this library," a claim nothing in this file set supports.
findings.source: columnstore.py:42 (`def column_subset(table: Table, include: Iterable[str]) -> list[Column]:`) contrasted with columnstore.py:67-69 (`encode_categoricals` calls only `should_encode`) and test_columnstore.py:14 (import list excludes `column_subset`)
findings.remedy: If column_subset genuinely has no other caller, delete it (dead code, subtractive fix); if it does have external callers elsewhere in the library, this variant should carry evidence of that (a caller or a test) rather than an unverifiable docstring assertion.

findings.claim: describe_source uses truthy `.get(key)` checks while effective_value uses presence (`in`) checks for the same env/project/user precedence, so the two functions disagree on any key whose value is present but falsy (e.g. an explicit empty-string override) -- directly contradicting this file's own documented contract that 'an explicitly empty string is a deliberate override, not an absence.' Concretely: with env={"retries": ""}, project={"retries": "5"}, effective_value("retries", ...) returns "" (respecting the env override) but describe_source("retries", ...) returns "project" (wrong layer, since "" is falsy and gets skipped).
findings.source: settings.py:5-8 (docstring: "A layer \"carries\" a key when the key is present, whatever the value -- an explicitly empty string is a deliberate override, not an absence.") vs settings.py:18 (`if key in env:`) and settings.py:28 (`if env.get(key):`) -- same pattern repeats at settings.py:20/30 (project) and settings.py:22/32 (user)
findings.remedy: Rewrite describe_source to use the same `key in <layer>` presence checks as effective_value (or, better, replace both functions' independent if-chains with one shared resolver -- e.g. iterate an ordered list of (name, layer) pairs and return the first layer where `key in layer` holds -- so effective_value and describe_source derive from a single owner of the precedence rule instead of two hand-maintained copies that can drift). Add a regression test with a falsy-but-present override (empty string or "0") to lock this in, since none of the existing tests use anything but truthy values.

findings.claim: ORDER is declared at module scope but never referenced by either function; effective_value and describe_source each hardcode the same three-layer sequence independently via separate if-chains instead of deriving from ORDER. This is the structural reason the two functions were free to drift in the first place (see the describe_source finding above).
findings.source: settings.py:14 (`ORDER = ("env", "project", "user")`), unused by settings.py:17-24 and settings.py:27-34
findings.remedy: Drive both functions off ORDER (loop over it to find the first layer that carries the key), or delete ORDER if a shared resolver replaces the hardcoded sequences -- either way, stop maintaining the layer order in three separate places (the constant plus two independent if-chains).
